ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)  -- A suspected missile strike from a U.S. Predator drone killed at least four people in a house in Pakistan's North Waziristan region early Saturday. Marchers protest recent U.S. missile strikes on the Pakistani tribal areas. The attack, which occurred in the Mir Ali subdivision in the village of Ali Khel, was one of several to hit the country Saturday. Six people were injured in Saturday's attack, the fourth suspected U.S. strike on Pakistani soil in November. The names of the victims have not been released. It is also not known why the house was targeted. Elsewhere, three people were killed and 11 were injured in an explosion inside a mosque in northwest Pakistan's tribal region, a government official said. The explosion happened just after 4 p.m. (6 a.m. ET), leaving the Hangu district mosque inside Pakistan's North-West Frontier Province in ruins, said Omer Faraz Khan, deputy superintendent of Hangu. He said rescuers were trying to save people trapped under the debris. It was not immediately clear how many people were inside the mosque at the time of the blast. Police were investigating the explosion, which was detonated using a homemade timer, Khan said. Hours later, three bombs exploded about 10 p.m. (noon ET) outside a stadium in Lahore where a music festival was being held, police Inspector Muntzir Kazmi said. A 13-year-old was injured, but it was unknown whether the victim was a boy or girl. This week, Pakistan's Foreign Ministry summoned U.S. Ambassador Anne Patterson to lodge a formal protest against another suspected U.S. missile strike on its territory, an act Pakistan Prime Minister Yousaf Raza Gilani called a violation of his nation's sovereignty.  Watch Gilani say his country has had enough of U.S. attacks » . Wednesday's strike in the Bannu region of Pakistan's North-West Frontier Province left five dead and seven wounded. That attack was farther inside Pakistani territory than previous attacks. The attack targeted a home outside the tribal areas that U.S. intelligence says have become a haven for Taliban and al Qaeda fighters battling U.S. and NATO troops in neighboring Afghanistan. The U.S. government has not acknowledged hitting targets within Pakistan, an ally in the war on al Qaeda launched after the September 11 attacks on New York and Washington. However, Pakistan's government has repeatedly complained about the strikes. Gilani took to the floor of the parliament and renewed his condemnation of the attacks Thursday but added that he thinks they will be controlled when President-elect Barack Obama takes office. In October, the foreign ministry summoned Patterson to lodge a "strong" protest on continuing missile attacks and said they should be stopped immediately. At the time, a missile strike from a suspected U.S. drone on a compound in South Waziristan killed 20 people. Pakistan's government said the attacks cost lives and undermine public support for its counterterrorism efforts. The U.S.-led coalition and NATO, based in Afghanistan, have been seeking a way to effectively battle militants who are launching attacks from Pakistan's swath of tribal areas along the border. They have become frustrated with Islamabad over the years, saying it is not being active enough against militants, a claim Pakistan denies. The United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from drones, which are controlled remotely.

# Suspected US Drone Strike Kills Four in North Waziristan Amid Wave of Violence Across Pakistan

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — A suspected US Predator drone strike killed four people in Pakistan's restive North Waziristan tribal region on Sunday, security officials said, as a series of attacks across the country left several others dead and wounded.

## The North Waziristan Strike

The drone fired two missiles at a compound in the Datta Khel area, roughly 40 kilometers west of Miranshah, the main town in North Waziristan, according to intelligence officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

"The missiles struck the compound early in the morning," one security official said. "Four people were killed, and the building was partially destroyed."

The identities of those killed were not immediately clear, and it remained uncertain whether any senior militants were among the dead. Datta Khel has long been considered a stronghold for militant networks operating along the border with Afghanistan.

North Waziristan, part of Pakistan's semi-autonomous tribal belt, has been a frequent target of the covert US drone program aimed at dismantling militant groups accused of launching cross-border attacks on coalition forces in Afghanistan.

The US government rarely comments publicly on individual drone strikes, and Pakistan officially condemns the operations as violations of its sovereignty, even as officials have privately cooperated with the program in the past.

## Violence Elsewhere in the Country

The drone strike came on a day marked by multiple incidents of violence across Pakistan.

In the northwestern city of Peshawar, a roadside bomb targeting a security convoy wounded several people, including two paramilitary soldiers, local police reported. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the blast.

Meanwhile, in the southwestern province of Balochistan, gunmen opened fire on a checkpoint, triggering an exchange of gunfire with security forces. Officials said at least one attacker was killed, though details remained sparse as the area was cordoned off.

Separately, authorities in the port city of Karachi reported that targeted shootings claimed additional lives amid ongoing political and ethnic tensions that have plagued Pakistan's largest city for years.

## A Country Under Strain

The attacks underscore the persistent security challenges facing Pakistan, a nuclear-armed nation that has been battling a homegrown insurgency for years while navigating a complicated relationship with the United States.

Militant groups, including the Pakistani Taliban, have carried out numerous attacks on both military and civilian targets, and the tribal regions along the Afghan border remain among the most volatile areas in the country.

Human rights organizations have repeatedly raised concerns about civilian casualties resulting from drone strikes, while Pakistani officials have warned that the operations fuel anti-American sentiment and complicate counterterrorism cooperation.

Officials said investigations into Sunday's incidents were ongoing.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Pakistan Protests US Drone Strikes as Tensions Mount Over Tribal Region Operations

**ISLAMABAD** — Relations between Pakistan and the United States came under renewed strain Thursday as Prime Minister Yousaf Raza Gilani's government lodged a formal diplomatic protest over continued American drone strikes in the country's northwestern tribal regions, describing the attacks as violations of Pakistani sovereignty.

The Foreign Ministry summoned US Ambassador Anne Patterson to convey the government's "deep concern" over the missile strikes, which have killed suspected militants but also caused civilian casualties in the semi-autonomous tribal belt bordering Afghanistan.

"These attacks are counterproductive and result in the loss of innocent lives," Gilani told reporters in Islamabad. "We have repeatedly conveyed to our American partners that such actions undermine our common objectives and inflame anti-American sentiment among our people."

The prime minister emphasized that Pakistan remained committed to fighting terrorism but insisted that operations on Pakistani soil must be conducted by Pakistani forces.

"We are a sovereign nation, and our sovereignty must be respected," Gilani said. "The war against extremism is our own war, but we will fight it on our own terms and with our own strategy."

## Diplomatic Friction

Officials familiar with the meeting between Foreign Ministry representatives and Ambassador Patterson said the Pakistani side pressed for greater intelligence-sharing and demanded that any counterterrorism operations be brought under Pakistani control.

"The ambassador was told in clear terms that these unilateral strikes complicate our efforts to build public support for counterterrorism operations," a senior Foreign Ministry official said on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly.

The US Embassy declined to comment on the specifics of the diplomatic exchange, with a spokesperson stating only that Washington "values its partnership with Pakistan and remains committed to working together against shared threats."

## A Delicate Balance

The drone campaign has placed Gilani's civilian government in a difficult position, caught between a powerful American ally that provides billions in aid and a domestic population increasingly hostile to what many view as foreign military intervention.

Political analysts note that public anger over the strikes has strengthened opposition parties and complicated the government's ability to cooperate openly with Washington.

"The government faces a genuine dilemma," said one Islamabad-based security analyst. "It cannot be seen as endorsing attacks that kill Pakistani citizens, yet it depends heavily on American support."

The tribal regions of North and South Waziristan have been the primary focus of the drone campaign, areas that Washington considers safe havens for militants launching attacks against coalition forces in neighboring Afghanistan.

Despite the public protests, questions persist about the extent of private cooperation between the two governments, with some observers suggesting Pakistani authorities may quietly tolerate strikes they condemn publicly.

Gilani rejected such characterizations, insisting his government's opposition was genuine and consistent.

"There is no ambiguity in our position," he said. "We have raised this matter at every level, and we will continue to do so until our concerns are addressed."

The latest tensions come at a sensitive moment for bilateral relations, as both nations attempt to coordinate strategy against militant networks operating along the porous Afghan-Pakistani frontier.

*— Reporting from Islamabad*

The Foreign Ministry has repeatedly lodged protests over drone operations, arguing that they inflame anti-American sentiment, undermine efforts to counter militancy, and cause civilian casualties. Officials have long maintained that the strikes are counterproductive and that Pakistan is capable of conducting its own operations against militants on its soil.

"These attacks are a violation of our territorial integrity," a government spokesman has said in response to previous strikes, echoing a position that has become a recurring point of friction between the two allies.

## A Complicated Alliance

Pakistan remains a key, if uneasy, U.S. ally in the campaign against al Qaeda, a partnership forged in the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, attacks. The country has received billions of dollars in American assistance and has lost thousands of soldiers and civilians in its own fight against militants.

Yet the relationship has been repeatedly tested by drone strikes, cross-border incidents, and mutual suspicions. Washington has at times accused elements within Pakistan of maintaining ties to militant groups, while Islamabad has accused the United States of failing to respect its sovereignty and of shifting the burden of the conflict onto Pakistani soil.

The tribal belt along the Afghan frontier has for years served as a haven for al Qaeda, the Pakistani Taliban, and other militant factions, making it a focal point of both U.S. counterterrorism efforts and Pakistani military operations.

## Rising Tensions

Analysts warned that the latest violence could deepen the rift between the two governments and further complicate an already fragile alliance. Public pressure on Pakistani leaders to take a harder line against drone strikes has grown, even as security cooperation continues behind the scenes.

Officials in Islamabad have called for greater intelligence sharing and for control over any operations conducted on Pakistani territory. Washington has defended the drone program as a vital tool against militants who threaten both countries and the broader region.

There was no immediate comment from U.S. officials on the reported strike.

Authorities said investigations into the bombings were underway, and security has been tightened across the region. The death toll from the day's violence was expected to rise as more information emerged from the remote and often inaccessible areas where the attacks occurred.
